title: The BoJ is late again
abstract: The Bank of Japan is late again, and I'm tired of pretending otherwise.
body:
## The BoJ is late again

I've been watching the Bank of Japan for years, and I've come to a conclusion: they are chronically late. Not fashionably late, not strategically late, but embarrassingly, predictably late. The kind of late that makes you wonder if they even own a watch. And here we are, on 2026-09-20, and they're still dithering. It's almost impressive how consistently they miss the moment.

## A history of missing the boat

Remember when everyone thought the BoJ would be the first to normalize? That was cute. While the Federal Reserve and the ECB were hiking, the BoJ sat on its hands, muttering about transitory inflation. Then when inflation finally showed up in Japan, they called it temporary. Then they called it external. Then they called it a mystery. Meanwhile, the yen went from bad to worse, and Japanese households started feeling the pinch. But the BoJ? They were still stuck in their deflationary mindset, clutching their yield curve control like a security blanket.

I get it. Japan has been fighting deflation for decades. The scars are real. But at some point, you have to recognize that the world has changed. The BoJ seems incapable of that. They're like a broken clock that's not even right twice a day. They're just wrong, all the time.

## The yield curve control trap

Yield curve control was a clever idea in theory. Cap bond yields, keep borrowing costs low, stimulate the economy. But in practice, it's been a disaster. The BoJ has become the buyer of last resort for Japanese government bonds, owning more than half the market. That's not monetary policy; that's nationalization of the bond market. And now they're trapped. If they raise the cap, yields spike, and the government's debt servicing costs explode. If they lower it, they lose even more credibility. So they do nothing. They tweak. They hint. They leak to the press. But they don't act.

Meanwhile, the yen has been in freefall. Import costs are soaring. Japanese consumers are paying more for everything from energy to food. And the BoJ? They're still talking about achieving a stable 2 percent inflation target. News flash: you've got inflation. It's just not the good kind. It's the kind that erodes living standards and makes everyone angry. But the BoJ doesn't seem to care. They're too busy patting themselves on the back for their 'comprehensive review' of monetary policy.

## The global context

It's not just Japan. Central banks everywhere have been late. The Fed called inflation transitory. The ECB was slow to hike. But the BoJ is in a league of its own. They've had decades of experience with deflation, and they still can't get it right. You'd think they'd have learned something. But no. They're still using the same playbook from the 1990s, and it's not working.

Part of the problem is the BoJ's obsession with credibility. They're so afraid of being seen as flip-flopping that they refuse to change course. But credibility isn't about stubbornness; it's about being right. And the BoJ has been wrong for years. They've been wrong about inflation, wrong about growth, wrong about the yen. At some point, you have to wonder if they're even trying.

## What should they do?

Honestly, I don't know. And that's the problem. Nobody knows. The BoJ has painted itself into a corner. They could abandon yield curve control and let the market set yields, but that would cause chaos. They could raise rates, but that would tank the economy. They could do nothing, but that's what they've been doing, and it's not working. The only thing they haven't tried is honesty. Maybe they should just admit they're out of ideas. That would at least be refreshing.

But they won't. They'll keep tweaking, keep hinting, keep leaking. They'll keep being late. And the rest of us will keep paying the price. The yen will keep falling. Prices will keep rising. And the BoJ will keep telling us that everything is under control. It's not. It hasn't been for a long time.

## The real cost of delay

The real cost of the BoJ's delay isn't just economic. It's human. It's the retiree who can't afford heating. It's the small business owner who can't import materials. It's the young worker who can't save because inflation is eating their wages. The BoJ's dithering has real consequences. And yet, they act like they have all the time in the world. They don't. Japan doesn't. The world doesn't.

So here we are, on 2026-09-20, and the BoJ is still late. I wish I could say I'm surprised. But I'm not. I've been watching them for too long. They're not going to change. They're going to keep being late until it's too late. And then they'll wonder what went wrong. But we'll know. We've always known.

## A final thought

Maybe I'm being too harsh. Maybe the BoJ is doing the best it can in impossible circumstances. But I don't buy it. They have tools. They have options. They just don't have the courage to use them. And that's the real tragedy. Not that they're late, but that they don't seem to care. They're not just late; they're indifferent. And that's worse.

So here's my advice to the BoJ: wake up. Look around. The world is changing. You can either change with it, or you can keep being late. But don't expect the rest of us to wait for you. We've been waiting for decades. We're done.
